title: Cask Ownership Programmes | Craft Beer School
desc: How distillery cask ownership programmes work, the costs and risks for buyers and distilleries plus what to check in India.
teaser: Selling casks to private buyers brings cash in early. It also brings legal, excise and trust questions that need answers first.
standfirst: Many new distilleries offer private buyers the chance to own a cask of their whisky. Done well, it funds the wait and builds loyal fans. Done badly, it creates disappointed buyers and regulatory trouble. Here is how these programmes work and what both sides should check.
sections:
The distillery fills a cask with new make spirit and sells it to a private buyer. The cask stays in the distillery's bonded warehouse while it matures. After an agreed number of years, the buyer can have it bottled, sell it back or sometimes sell it on. Fees usually cover storage, insurance and bottling.

For the distillery, it brings cash before the whisky is ready. For the buyer, it offers a personal connection to the distillery and their own bottles at the end. The appeal is real. So are the complications.

A cask contains untaxed spirit in bond. The buyer owns the spirit, but it stays under excise control until duty is paid. Every year, some of it evaporates. A 200 litre barrel filled at 63.5% ABV holds 127 litres of pure alcohol. After several years in Indian heat, where losses run well above the roughly 2% a year often quoted for Scotland, the buyer will have noticeably less.

Buyers should understand from the start that the volume will fall and the strength will change. A clear agreement explains this. The distillery should regauge and report on the cask regularly. Our guide to whisky maturation and casks explains what happens inside.

In India, the sale and movement of alcohol is tightly controlled by each state. Selling untaxed spirit in bond to a private individual raises questions that differ by state: whether it is allowed at all, how ownership is recorded, how duty is paid when the cask is bottled and whether the buyer can take bottles home from another state.

Before launching a cask programme, a distillery needs clear advice from a licensing consultant and a lawyer who knows the state's excise rules. Buyers should ask the distillery to show how the programme meets those rules. If the answer is vague, that is a warning sign.
Costs both sides should see clearly

• The price of the cask and its fill.
  • Yearly storage and insurance fees.
  • Regauging and sampling fees.
  • Bottling, labelling and packaging costs at the end.
  • Excise duty and taxes when the whisky is bottled for release.
  • Transport, if the buyer wants bottles delivered elsewhere.

A buyer who sees only the cask price will be surprised later. A good programme publishes every cost up front.
Cask investment is not a promise

Some cask sellers market casks as investments with high returns. Be very careful with that. Whisky values are not guaranteed. Casks can leak, the spirit can mature poorly and resale markets can be thin. Financial regulators, including in the UK, have warned consumers about cask investment schemes.

A distillery should never promise a return. It should sell the cask as what it is: a chance to own and eventually bottle your own whisky. Buyers who want an investment should take independent financial advice.

For a distillery, a good cask programme is a long relationship. Keep a cask register with fill date, spirit, cask type, volume and strength. Send owners an annual update, ideally with a sample. Invite them for a visit. When it is time to bottle, offer clear choices on strength and labelling. Our guide to how whisky is made is a useful thing to share with new owners.

Limit the number of casks sold so private casks do not take over stock you need for your own releases.
Choosing the cask type for a programme

The cask a buyer gets shapes the whisky they eventually bottle. Most programmes offer a small range: an ex-bourbon barrel of around 200 litres, a hogshead of around 250 litres and sometimes a sherry seasoned cask. Smaller casks have more wood contact per litre and mature faster, which in Indian heat can mean strong wood flavour within a few years.

Be clear with buyers about what each choice means. An ex-bourbon barrel tends to give vanilla and sweet spice. A sherry cask brings dried fruit and colour. A first fill cask gives more flavour than a refill.

Offer only casks you would happily use for your own releases. A programme that fills poor casks to keep costs down produces poor whisky. Years later, buyers will bottle it with your name on the label.

If you run a distillery, write the full cost sheet a buyer would see, from filling to bottled whisky. Test it with two or three potential buyers. If you are thinking of buying, ask the distillery for that sheet and their excise position in writing. Either way, understanding maturation and cask behaviour is what lets you judge whether the promise holds.
faqs: Can I own a cask of whisky in India?
It depends on the state's excise rules, which control the sale and movement of untaxed spirit. Ask the distillery how its programme meets current rules.
Does whisky in a cask lose volume?
Yes. Spirit evaporates through the wood every year. The loss in Indian heat is well above the roughly 2% a year often quoted for Scotland.
Is buying a cask a good investment?
Returns are not guaranteed. Treat a cask as a chance to own your own whisky. Take independent advice before buying one as an investment.
